prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The wall fills the forward view in frames 1–3, roughly 1–3 m away, with the triangular climbing volumes projecting nearer than the wall; a person is partly visible very close at the lower-left edge of frame 1. In frames 4–5, that person occupies the near foreground, approximately 0.4–1 m from the camera wearer, while the wall and floor mat remain behind them at roughly 1–3 m; the bright silhouette also makes the person's arm extending to the right in frame 5 clearer than in RGB. Across the strip, the viewpoint turns right and/or approaches the person, so the wall feature shifts out of view and the person grows from partial to dominant, with the head and lower body increasingly cropped. The map clarifies near–far layering and protrusion from the wall, but its metre estimates are uncertain, and the large saturated bright areas, soft boundaries, and black gaps around the person make fine limb distances and occlusions unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map separates a nearby person from the wall-mounted triangular volume in frame 1, shows no confident instances in frame 2, and separates the triangular feature from a large wall/background region in frame 3. In frames 4–5, one person is segmented in the near foreground, about 0.4–1 m from the camera wearer and in front of the wall and mat; the person shifts from the left side of frame 4 to filling most of frame 5, with the head, legs, and parts of the right arm outside the image. The RGB indicates the person is generally facing the camera wearer, with their torso angled slightly sideways in frame 4 and more front-facing in frame 5; no second fully visible person is isolated. The masks make occlusion boundaries and image-edge truncation easier to see, but labels such as “tie,” “key,” “stop sign,” and “umbrella,” plus the oversized green region, are plainly unreliable and do not support those object identities or precise distances.
descriptions.pose: No usable body or hand skeleton appears in frames 1–3, so this map adds almost no spatial information about the partly visible person in frame 1 or the wall features. In frame 4, a yellow upper-body skeleton places one nearby person roughly 0.5–1 m ahead, with the head above the torso and bent arm segments extending across the upper body; the lower body is not recovered, so stance and exact reach cannot be determined. In frame 5, only a small magenta hand cluster is detected near the person's upper-right side, indicating a hand close to the camera wearer and plausibly within arm's reach, while the rest of the body remains untracked despite being visible in RGB. The detections suggest the person turns or moves closer as the viewpoint shifts right, but missing joints, displaced keypoints, and the tiny isolated hand make facing direction, gaze, limb depth, and person-to-object distances unreliable.
